domain: Ohmline, a fictional public EV-charging network (a charge point operator). Ohmline runs about 300 charging sites (public car parks, workplaces and a bus depot), each with several charge points made by different vendors that talk to Ohmline over a simplified OCPP-1.6J-style JSON-over-WebSocket protocol. Drivers start a charge with an RFID card or the driver app (a .NET MAUI app that is its own bounded context, downstream of the server's Open Host Service, queuing commands offline and caching read models); Ohmline must keep every site under the power limit of its grid connection (minus any curtailment the grid operator requests), price each session from the tariff locked at its start (time-of-use bands in site-local time, session fee, idle fee after a grace period), and take payment through a pre-authorize/capture/void payment provider. The core domain (Charging: ChargePoint, ChargingSession and the ChargingJourney process manager; Site Energy: SitePowerBudget and its fair-share allocator) has real, quantitative, time-dependent invariants; supporting contexts are Tariffs (a Knowledge Level), Driver Accounts (token uniqueness) and Billing (deliberately plain CRUD with an outbox, no actors); the Device Gateway is the anticorruption layer to the chargers. External systems are all fictional and simulated in the sample: TallyPay (payment provider, ugly API), Northgate Grid (grid operator demand-response feed), AssetTrack (a legacy asset registry exported as messy CSV: the Big Ball of Mud) and a roaming hub (Conformist / Separate Ways, documentation only). Charge points are long-lived, connected, timer-driven devices and every session, site and token is a natural single-writer entity, which makes the domain a natural fit for sharded persistent actors.

chapters.title: The Aggregate as a Persistent Actor: Commands, Events and the Journal
chapters.summary: Puts the deciders inside Akka.Persistence and follows one command all the way to disk. The shell owns identity, concurrency, durability, time and messaging; replies are wire-safe closed records (and the union-on-the-wire trap is shown); a System.Text.Json manifest serializer is in place before the first persisted event. The command -> Decide -> PersistAll -> journal write -> Evolve -> reply cycle is drawn as a sequence diagram, and the chapter shows exactly what the actor does while a write is in flight (the internal stash), how Persist, PersistAsync, PersistAll and DeferAsync differ and which ordering guarantees each gives, what really lands in the SQLite journal (a guided tour of real rows), why the single-writer guarantee lets sequence numbers replace optimistic locks and what the sequence-number conflict looks like if two incarnations ever write, and finally a reusable DeciderActor for the other aggregates. Chapter 11 continues with recovery, snapshots, Durable State, failure and testing.

sections.title: While the write is in flight: the internal stash
sections.summary: Between PersistAll and its last callback the actor handles no new command: Akka.Persistence parks every incoming message in an internal stash (separate from IWithStash) and unstashes them in arrival order after the callbacks, so a slow journal becomes mailbox latency, never a race; a second sequence diagram shows two commands overlapping one slow write. The guarantees per persistence id: events are written in the order Decide returned them, callbacks run in that order, and no command observes a half-applied decision. Costs: the internal stash is unbounded by default and the configured internal-stash-overflow-strategy throws when a bound is set; a slow database backs up every mailbox it serves; Sender is stable inside callbacks, but capturing it is still the house style.

sections.title: Persist, PersistAsync, PersistAll and DeferAsync
sections.summary: The four write calls compared in one table: stashing or not, callback order, throughput and when each is right. PersistAsync does not stash, so a later command can be decided against state whose earlier event has not been applied yet: wrong for a decider, right for a high-rate recorder of facts that never rejects anything. DeferAsync runs a handler after every preceding PersistAsync has completed, without writing anything. PersistAll keeps one decision atomic (one AtomicWrite: all of its events or none), which is why AK1006 asks for it instead of a loop of Persist calls; the async-handler and onComplete overloads arrived in 1.5.57. The house rule: deciders always use PersistAll.

sections.title: One writer per persistence id: sequence numbers instead of locks
sections.summary: The single-writer guarantee (one live incarnation per persistence id, which sharding and the split-brain resolver provide in Chapter 12) means Decide always sees every earlier event, so the expected-version checks of a database-backed repository are unnecessary inside the aggregate: the actor is the lock and the sequence number is the aggregate's version (the Version in every CommandAccepted). An expected version still belongs where a person decided from a stale screen (section 19.3). If two incarnations ever did write, both recover to sequence n and both try to write n + 1; the journal's uniqueness on (persistence_id, sequence_number) rejects the second write, OnPersistFailure stops that actor and its stashed commands become dead letters; writer_uuid and the replay filter (repair-by-discard-old) protect later reads. This is a safety net, not a concurrency strategy (section 21.8: never two writers).

chapters.title: Recovery, Snapshots, Durable State and Failure
chapters.summary: Follows a persistent aggregate through the rest of its life. Recovery in depth (snapshot offer, replay through Evolve only, RecoveryCompleted, the stash during recovery) drawn as a sequence diagram; snapshots as a cache with a cost model; recovery at scale (max-concurrent-recoveries, recovery storms, the journal circuit breaker) and recovery failure (the poison event); timers re-armed from recovered state; a preview of the passivation-and-rehydration lifecycle that Chapter 12 automates; failure semantics (domain errors versus infrastructure failures, persist failure versus rejection, what happens to stashed commands); Durable State as the non-event-sourced alternative, which Akka.NET 1.5.73 does not ship, compared honestly and built the Akka.NET way for a supporting ChargePointListing; and testing the shell with Akka.Persistence.TestKit's scriptable journal and snapshot store.

sections.title: Recovery in depth
sections.summary: What happens between an actor's construction and its first command, as a mermaid sequence diagram: the snapshot store offers the latest snapshot (none yet), the journal replays the remaining events in sequence order through Recover handlers (Evolve only: never Decide, never a reply, never a side effect), then RecoveryCompleted arrives; commands that arrive meanwhile wait in the internal stash; IsRecovering, LastSequenceNr and SnapshotSequenceNr; recovery-event-timeout (30 s by default) and Akka.Persistence.Sql's replay-batch-size (1,000); why a total, deterministic Evolve (section 7.5) is what makes replay safe.

sections.title: Recovery at scale: throttling, storms and the poison event
sections.summary: After a node restart hundreds of charge points recover at once; akka.persistence.max-concurrent-recoveries (default 50) makes the rest wait so the database is not stampeded; estimating a recovery storm (entities x events / replay rate) and how snapshots and passivation shrink it; the journal circuit breaker (max-failures 10, call-timeout 10 s, reset-timeout 30 s). OnRecoveryFailure: an unreadable event, an unknown manifest or a journal outage stops the actor, and a sharded entity is started again by its next message and fails again (the poison event); the runbook: fix the serializer or add an upcaster, never edit the row.

sections.title: Passivation and rehydration: an entity's life
sections.summary: A preview of the lifecycle Chapter 12 automates, drawn as a stateDiagram-v2: created by its first message, recovering, serving commands, idle, passivated (the shard asks it to stop with a hand-off message so nothing in flight is lost), absent from memory but whole in the journal, rehydrated by the next message from its snapshot plus the tail. What this means for memory (only active entities are resident), for timers (a passivated reservation still expires because section 11.4 re-arms timers on recovery) and for recovery storms (section 11.3); why PoisonPill and Context.Stop are wrong for persistent entities (section 12.4).

sections.title: Failure semantics: errors versus failures
sections.summary: Domain rejections are values and replies; a persist failure stops the actor (backoff supervisor or sharding restart) and the commands stashed behind the failed write become dead letters, so their senders time out and retry with the same idempotency key (section 12.6); a persist rejection (for example a serialization error) keeps the actor alive; a sequence diagram of each; never PoisonPill a persistent actor.

sections.title: Durable State: the non-event-sourced alternative
sections.summary: Not every aggregate needs its history. JVM Akka's Durable State keeps only the latest state with a revision number in a DurableStateStore; Akka.NET 1.5.73 (and 1.6.0-beta5) ship no Durable State store, which the editor checked against the assemblies and NuGet on 2026-11-04. The section compares the options honestly in one table (history, queries through projections, storage growth, schema evolution, concurrency): event sourcing; state sourcing on the journal (persist the whole new state as one event, snapshot after every write, delete what came before); a state-stored repository behind an actor with optimistic concurrency on a revision column; and no actor at all (Billing, section 16.3). The supporting ChargePointListing (display name, access instructions such as 'Level -2, bays 14-19', opening hours) is built the state-sourced way and is later shown in the driver app. The rule: choose by whether anyone will ever ask what happened, not by convenience.

chapters.part: Part V: CQRS, Processes and Integration
chapters.title: CQRS I: From Journal to Read Model
chapters.summary: Answers questions without asking aggregates, and shows every moving part between a persisted event and a query result: why the write model cannot serve queries; the whole write -> journal -> query journal -> projection -> read store -> query API pipeline drawn as one diagram; tagging; Persistence Query (EventsByPersistenceId, EventsByTag, their Current* variants and PersistenceIds) with Akka.Persistence.Sql's global, exclusive offsets; a resumable projection runner with at-least-once delivery; idempotent upserts with the offset stored in the same database transaction; running exactly one projector per projection in the cluster; what happens when a projection fails and restarts; and the first read models behind a query API. Chapter 14 covers living with the resulting eventual consistency.

sections.title: Why the write model cannot answer your questions
sections.summary: The 'ask every aggregate for the dashboard' anti-pattern (fan-out Asks, waking passivated entities, no query language over a journal of events); CQRS as separate models for writing and reading, not necessarily separate databases (Greg Young's definition), and why event sourcing makes it nearly unavoidable; the whole pipeline drawn as one mermaid diagram (command -> aggregate -> journal; journal -> query journal -> projection -> read store -> query endpoint) with the three places where latency and failure live; read-your-writes from the entity versus lagging views, previewing Chapter 14.

sections.title: Tagging events
sections.summary: An IWriteEventAdapter that returns Tagged; tag design (charging, charging-session, site-energy) and why tags are durable vocabulary; TagTable mode in Akka.Persistence.Sql; the tags rows appear in the journal tour.
sections.codeChange: Add Charging.Actors/Persistence/ChargingTagger and SiteEnergy.Actors/Persistence/SiteEnergyTagger (IWriteEventAdapter returning Tagged with tags per event type); register via journal builder AddWriteEventAdapter in each AddXxxContext; tests; extend JournalTourTests to assert the tags rows (ordering_id, tag, persistence_id, sequence_nr) written for a ChargePoint event.

sections.title: Persistence Query: the read side of the journal
sections.summary: The read journal as a stream API over the same tables: EventsByPersistenceId versus CurrentEventsByPersistenceId (live versus finite), EventsByTag and CurrentEventsByTag, PersistenceIds; the EventEnvelope (offset, persistence id, sequence number, event, timestamp); Akka.Persistence.Sql's offsets are the global ordering column and are exclusive; polling under the hood (refresh-interval and the journal-sequence-retrieval gap detection), which is where lag comes from (tuned in section 14.3); never dispose the shared system materializer in 1.5.

sections.title: A resumable projection runner: offsets and at-least-once
sections.summary: A projection is a stream from a stored offset to a handler: load the offset, run EventsByTag from it, handle each envelope, store the new offset; RestartSource.OnFailuresWithBackoff and a UniqueKillSwitch; storing the offset after the handler gives at-least-once delivery, storing it before gives at-most-once and silently lost updates; a sequence diagram of a crash between the read-model write and the offset save.

Create branch wrong/ch13-s04-offset-before-handler (offset saved first; the same crash loses the update).

sections.title: Idempotent read models: upserts and the offset in one transaction
sections.summary: Because delivery is at-least-once, every handler must tolerate duplicates: upsert keyed by the read model's own key and guarded by the source sequence number (update only if the incoming event is newer); the offset written in the same Npgsql transaction as the row so the two can never disagree; the per-row version that read-your-writes uses in section 14.1; SessionHistory as the first read model, with its row logic as a pure function.

sections.title: Running exactly one projector

sections.title: When a projection fails: restarts, poison events and lag
sections.summary: Transient failures (the database is down: back off and resume from the stored offset) versus permanent ones (a handler bug or an event it cannot handle: every restart fails on the same envelope, so the read model silently stops moving); choosing per projection between stopping loudly and recording and skipping; making a stuck projection visible by comparing its stored offset with the journal's highest ordering; restarting after a fix loses nothing, because the journal still holds every event.

chapters.part: Part V: CQRS, Processes and Integration
chapters.title: CQRS II: Living with Eventual Consistency
chapters.summary: Makes the lag between a write and a read a designed property instead of a surprise: read-your-writes using the version (sequence number) a command returns, a consistency choice for each screen, tuning and measuring projection lag, live push from projections with Server-Sent Events for browsers and SignalR for app clients (DistributedPubSub as the backplane), several read models built from one event stream including one shaped for the driver app that Chapter 19 consumes, testing projections, and a preview of rebuilding read models that Chapter 20 completes.

sections.title: Read-your-writes with the version a command returns
sections.summary: The reply already carries Version, the aggregate's sequence number (section 10.4), and every session-history row stores last_sequence_nr (section 13.5), so a query can ask for 'at least version n': the server answers from the read model once it has caught up, waits briefly, or says honestly that it has not caught up yet; the alternative of asking the aggregate itself (consistent, but one entity at a time and it wakes passivated entities); a sequence diagram of POST /sessions/{id}/stop -> 202 with version 7 -> GET /sessions/{id}?minVersion=7.

sections.title: Consistency choices per screen
sections.summary: Not every screen needs the same guarantee: a decision table over Ohmline's screens (operator site live board: eventual and pushed; driver's active session: read-your-writes, then pushed; receipt: eventual with a 'being prepared' state; connector availability before reserving: ask the aggregate, because being wrong strands a driver at a blocked connector); the three tools (aggregate query, read model with a minimum version, plain read model) and their costs; UX language for lag ('updating…') and never fake certainty.
sections.codeChange: Add docs/consistency-per-screen.md (table: screen, read source, guarantee, what the user sees while stale, owner).

sections.title: Tuning and measuring projection lag
sections.summary: Where the default 500-1200 ms lag comes from (journal polling plus sequence-gap detection); tuning both refresh-interval and journal-sequence-retrieval.query-delay (tuning one alone does nothing); the database cost of low lag; measuring lag as the time between an event's journal timestamp and the commit of the projection that handled it, instead of guessing; the number feeds Chapter 18's dashboards.

sections.title: Live push with Server-Sent Events

chapters.title: The Mobile Edge: An Offline-First .NET MAUI Driver App
chapters.summary: Answers the question 'does any of this belong in the mobile app, or only on the API side?' by building Ohmline's driver app with .NET MAUI. The domain (aggregates, invariants, event sourcing, actors) stays on the server; the app is its own bounded context downstream of the server's Open Host Service and speaks only a Published Language of shared client contracts, never aggregates. What does pay off on the phone: the ubiquitous language in the UI, value objects for input validation, client-generated command ids that the aggregate deduplicates, a durable SQLite outbox of pending commands drained by a single-reader Channel 'mailbox', a local SQLite cache of read models fed by the query side and SignalR, optimistic UI reconciled against server versions, and C# 15 unions for screen and command state. Persistence and CQRS on the server and on the phone are compared side by side; the chapter explains why Akka.NET does not belong on the phone today and when local-first event sourcing on the device is the right exception; and one trace runs from a tap on the phone to the journal. The client logic is a plain net11.0 library tested in the root solution; the thin MAUI head lives in its own solution under mobile/ and is built for net11.0-android at every tag from ch19-s04 on.

sections.title: Persistence and CQRS: the server versus the phone
sections.summary: A side-by-side table of what each side stores and why. On the server the journal is the source of truth, events and snapshots are kept, aggregates decide, projections derive read models, and the single writer is a sharded actor. On the phone nothing is the source of truth: the read-model cache is disposable (delete it and refill it from the server), the outbox is the only durable intent and holds commands rather than events, the app validates input but decides nothing, and the single reader is a Channel loop. Further rows: consistency (authoritative and immediate versus provisional until accepted), identity (sequence numbers versus client command ids and server versions), schema evolution (events forever versus a cache you can drop and an outbox you must drain or migrate across app upgrades), failure (supervision and recovery versus process death at the operating system's whim). The rule both sides share: commands are intent, events are fact, and only the server writes facts.

sections.title: Should the phone run actors? Local-first as the exception
sections.summary: The evidence: Akka.NET 1.5.73 runs under MAUI's default partial trimming but fails under full trimming and NativeAOT (ConfigurationErrorsException from System.Configuration inside ActorSystem.Create, measured on linux-x64), which AOT-compiled deployments such as iOS need; Akka.Hosting relies on hosted services that MAUI never starts, so AddAkka is unavailable; about 2.4 MB of extra assemblies and a scheduler that ticks every 10 ms; a process the OS may kill whenever it is in the background. The 1.6 betas trim and AOT-compile a trivial actor cleanly, and MAUI hosting support is in a draft pull request. The verdict: actor thinking yes, actor framework no on phones; a local actor system is reasonable on kiosks, desktops and edge boxes (a depot site controller on mains power and a trusted LAN). The genuine exception is local-first: when a device must decide while disconnected and its decisions must stand (a field technician's inspection log in a basement, collaborative offline edits), the device owns its own aggregate and event log and merges with CRDTs or server-side reconciliation; Ohmline's driver commands are not that case, because their invariants (one session per connector, the site's power budget) live in shared state no phone can see.
